No View Is the Whole

The World and the Ways We Make Sense of It

Soman Lin

所見非全貌

世界，以及我們理解它的方式

Soman Lin

Preface — Leaving a Gap

序　留一個空隙

Some books leave you holding more answers than you started with. This one is trying to do something smaller: to make you a little more alert to answers themselves.

I am not a sceptic about everything, and I have no interest in declaring that every position has its merits. What I distrust is a very short moment, about half a second long. We see something and give it a name. Having named it, we supply a cause. Having supplied a cause, we reach a verdict. Then we forget that we just took three steps. By the time we look up, the thing we built to make the world easier to handle has quietly become "that is simply how things are."

This happens well outside philosophy seminars. Engineers treat the test set as the deployment site. Managers treat the KPI as the health of the company. In an argument between two people, a single action becomes a personality within a few sentences. Somebody reads a powerful body of ideas and jumps straight from "this helps me live better" to "this must describe how the universe actually is." We are not short on intelligence, and we are not short on goodwill. What we lack is the habit of pausing for half a second to see which step we just took.

So this book does not begin with definitions. It begins with a few scenes you have probably been in yourself: a meeting where everybody insists they are stating facts; a model that performed beautifully in its old environment and failed quietly somewhere new; an argument where you understood every sentence the other person said and still felt the two of you lived in different worlds. And the hardest one to handle — the feeling that something is off, when you cannot say what.

Those scenes look unrelated. After sitting with them for a while I noticed they were all pressing me to answer the same question. When the world is far larger than my understanding of it, how do I use my understanding without being tied down by it?

My answer at the moment will not fit in a sentence. It is a loop. Start by admitting we can only reach the world through some representation. Then ask what that representation kept and what it discarded, and for what purpose. Then check the conditions under which it holds, and where it starts to fail. When you meet somebody else's representation, try to rebuild it before you translate it into your own language. And finally, compress the analysis into intuition, while keeping a way to unfold it again.

If this book works, you will not necessarily agree with me by the end. You may replace every term I use. What matters is something else: the next time you are very certain, very angry, very impressed by a theory, or very keen to settle a question, a small gap will open in your head. That gap gives you the chance to ask whether you are looking at the world, or at the world as it appears inside your model.

That gap is what this book is for.

有一種書，讀完之後你會多出很多答案。這本書想做的事情比較小：讓你對答案本身變得敏感一點。

我不是懷疑一切的人，也沒有興趣把所有立場都說成「各有道理」。我不信任的是一個很短的瞬間。那個瞬間大概只有半秒鐘：我們看見一件事，替它命名；命名之後，替它補上原因；補上原因之後，做出判斷；然後忘記自己剛才連走了三步。等回過神來，那個原本只是為了方便理解世界而做出來的東西，已經變成「事情本來就是這樣」。

這件事不只發生在哲學系的教室裡。工程師會把測試資料當成部署現場；主管會把 KPI 當成公司的健康狀況；夫妻吵架時，一次行為會在幾句話之內被說成人格；一個人讀到一套很有力量的思想，往往會直接從「它幫我活得比較好」跳到「它必然描述了宇宙真正的樣子」。我們不缺智力，也不缺善意。我們缺的是一個能讓自己停半秒、看見「我剛才到底做了哪一步」的習慣。

所以這本書不從定義開始。它從幾個你大概也遇過的場面開始：一場每個人都說自己在講事實的會議；一套在舊環境裡表現得很漂亮、換個地方就悄悄失效的模型；一場你聽懂了對方每一句話、卻仍然覺得你們住在不同世界的爭吵；還有那種最難處理的感覺——你說不出原因，但就是覺得哪裡不對。

這些場面看起來彼此無關。寫了一段時間之後我才發現，它們在逼我回答同一個問題：當世界比我的理解大得多的時候，我要怎麼使用自己的理解，而不被它綁住？

我目前的答案沒辦法用一句話講完。它是一套來回。先承認我們只能透過某種表示接近世界；接著問這個表示為了什麼目的留下什麼、丟掉什麼；然後檢查它在哪些條件下可靠、從哪裡開始失效；碰到別人的表示時，先試著把它重建起來，再考慮翻譯成自己的語言；最後，把一次次分析壓縮成直覺，同時替直覺留一條可以重新展開的路。

這本書如果成功，讀到最後你不一定同意我。你甚至可能把我用的每個詞都換掉。要緊的是另一件事：下一次當你很確定、很生氣、很佩服某套理論、很想替某件事下結論的時候，你腦中會多出一個很小的空隙。那個空隙讓你有機會問一句：我現在看見的是世界，還是世界在我這套模型裡的樣子？

那個空隙，就是這本書想留下來的東西。

Part One

Seeing Your Own Lens

We assume we are looking at the world. Later we find out that attention, language, purpose, and models have been sitting in between the whole time. Part One tries to make those layers visible again. Once you can see your own lens, you can start telling the two apart: which part is the world pushing back, and which part is the processing we did in order to understand it.

第一部

看見自己的鏡頭

我們以為自己在看世界。後來才發現，中間一直隔著注意力、語言、目的和模型。第一部想做的事，是把這幾層中介重新變得看得見。只要能看見自己的鏡頭，就能開始分辨：哪一段是世界頂回來的，哪一段是我們為了理解而加工出來的。

1 — Everyone Is Talking About "the Facts"

第一章　每個人都在說「事實」

The layer hardest to see is usually the one we added ourselves.

最難看見的那一層，通常是我們自己替世界加上去的。

The meeting was set for ten. At three minutes past, the last person pushed the door open, put down a laptop, and said nothing.

It was a small thing. Three minutes.

An hour later, when we broke up, those three minutes had grown into three separate worlds.

In the corridor the project manager told me the team had no discipline about schedules at all. Back at his desk, the engineer's first words were that the previous meeting had run late and he had posted about it in the group chat before ten. In the afternoon a colleague walked past with a coffee and described something else again: everyone had been strung tight lately, which was why small things were getting amplified.

Put the three accounts side by side and something odd shows up. All three people believed they were reporting what happened. What they were reporting were three different kinds of thing.

Ten oh three is a record. The previous meeting running late is another record, plus a causal thread. "No discipline" is a category. "Everyone is strung tight" is an explanation sitting at a higher level. All four can be partly true at once, and they can support or contradict each other. The one thing they cannot do is sit on the same layer.

Kurosawa's Rashomon, from 1950, is about exactly this. A samurai is found dead in a grove, and four people tell the story of that day in turn: the bandit, the samurai's wife, the dead man speaking through a medium, and a woodcutter who was hiding behind a tree. All four accounts are complete, all four carry feeling, all four hold together internally, and all four contradict each other. The film never tells you who lied. What it shows you is that each account is that event after it has passed through one person's position, fear, and self-regard.

The film gave Chinese a word. When we say a situation "has become a Rashomon," we are usually complaining that the truth is unavailable. What the word actually points at is something else: each person reported their own layer honestly.

Our everyday understanding goes off the rails often, and the reason is not that people lack logic. It is that these layers happen in the head far too fast. The eye catches an expression, and "he is impatient" has already surfaced. A message goes unanswered for three hours, and within seconds the story becomes "he does not think I matter." A model gets something badly wrong on a new batch of data and we say the model is broken. Revenue falls and we say the market has gone bad.

會議約十點。十點零三分，最後一個人推門進來，把筆電放下，沒說話。

事情很小。三分鐘而已。

一小時後散會，這三分鐘已經長成三個世界。

專案經理佩宜在走廊上跟我說：「這團隊對時程根本沒有紀律。」工程師建宏回到座位第一句話是：「上一場會延誤，我十點前就在群組講了。」下午雅琪端著咖啡經過，講的又是另一件事：「大家最近繃得很緊，所以這種小事才會被放大。」

把三句話擺在一起，會出現一個很奇怪的現象。三個人都認為自己在講「發生了什麼」，可他們講的其實是三種不同的東西。

十點零三分是一筆紀錄。上一場會延誤是另一筆紀錄，外加一條因果線索。「沒有紀律」是一個分類。「大家繃得很緊」是一個更高層的解釋。這四樣東西可以同時各有一部分成立，也可以互相支援或互相打架；它們唯一不能做的事，是被當成同一層。

黑澤明一九五〇年的《羅生門》講的就是這件事。一名武士死在竹林裡，四個人分別把當天的事說了一遍：強盜、武士的妻子、透過靈媒說話的死者，以及躲在樹後的樵夫。四段敘述都很完整，都有情緒，都自成道理，卻互相矛盾。電影沒有告訴你誰在說謊。它讓你看見的是：每個人講出來的，都是那場事件通過自己的位置、恐懼和自尊之後留下的版本。這部片後來變成中文裡的一個詞。我們說一件事「變成羅生門」，通常是在抱怨真相不明；但這個詞真正指出來的，是每個人都誠實地報告了自己那一層。

我們日常的理解之所以常常失控，原因並不是人沒有邏輯。是因為這些層次在腦中發生得太快。眼睛看到一個表情，腦裡已經浮出「他不耐煩」；訊息隔了三小時才回，幾秒鐘之內故事就變成「他不重視我」；模型在一批新資料上錯得很難看，我們說「模型壞了」；營收往下掉，我們說「市場不行了」。

Any one of those sentences might turn out to be right. The trouble is that each of them has travelled several steps past the original observation, and none of those steps left a receipt.

這些句子每一句都可能最後被證明有道理。麻煩的地方在於，它們都比原始觀察多走了好幾步，而那幾步沒有留下收據。

The eye is already selecting

眼睛從一開始就在挑東西

People cannot record the world the way a camera does. A camera is not especially honest either. Focal length, exposure, sensor, sampling rate — every one of them is deciding what gets kept. With human senses and attention it is more obvious still.

Stand four people on the same street. The architect is looking at the proportions of the façades, the taxi driver at the gaps in the traffic, the police officer at whose walk is slightly wrong. The five-year-old sees only the dog by the kerb. The street did not split into four streets. One street, filtered through four different sets of attention and purpose, yields four usable representations.

So "observation" was never unprocessed. It is processed a few layers less than "explanation."

That distinction matters, because we are in the habit of hiding the processing inside the tone of voice. "He did not reply to me today" and "he is pulling away from me" differ by a few words, and the second one has an entire model of a relationship packed inside it. Once that model gets stated as a fact, it no longer has to compete with any other explanation.

Mature understanding does not ban inference. Without inference we could not do anything at all. It asks for one thing only: inference can be fast, but it should not quietly pass itself off as observation.

There is a small exercise that makes this concrete. Think of something recent that made you angry, and write down the sentence you feel most sure of. Suppose it is: "My manager has no respect at all for my expertise." Now you are not allowed to use the words respect, expertise, or at all. You may write only what a camera and a microphone could have recorded. You might end up with something like this: after I raised the risk, he asked no follow-up questions; five minutes later he decided to go with a different option.

The new version is not necessarily truer. What it does is take the story apart for a moment, so you can see the square where the story was added.

人沒有辦法像攝影機那樣把世界錄下來。攝影機本身也沒有那麼老實：焦段、曝光、感光元件、取樣頻率，每一項都在決定什麼被留下。人的感官和注意力更明顯。

站在同一條街上，建築師在看立面比例，計程車司機在看車流縫隙，警察在看誰的走路方式不太對，五歲的小孩只看見路邊那隻狗。這條街沒有因此裂成四條街。同一條街，經過四套不同的注意與目的，被切出四種可用的表示。

所謂「觀察」，從來就不是零加工。它只是比「解釋」少幾層加工。

這個區分很重要，因為我們習慣把加工藏在語氣裡。「他今天沒有回我訊息」和「他在疏遠我」聽起來只差幾個字，後面那句已經裝進一整套關係模型。當這套模型被說成事實，它就不必再跟其他解釋競爭。

成熟的理解不會禁止推論。沒有推論，我們什麼都做不了。它只要求一件事：推論可以很快，但別偷偷冒充觀察。

有個很小的練習可以體會這件事。回想最近一件讓你生氣的事，把腦中最確定的那句話寫下來。假設它是：「主管根本不尊重我的專業。」接下來不准使用「尊重」「專業」「根本」這幾個詞，只能寫攝影機和錄音機可能記到的東西。你也許會得到這樣一段：「我提出風險之後，他沒有追問；五分鐘後他直接決定採用另一個方案。」

新的版本不見得比較「真」。它做的事只是把故事暫時拆開，讓你看見故事是在哪一格被加上去的。

"I don't know" can be said precisely

「不知道」可以講得很精確

People have an odd fear of the unknown, as though admitting "I don't know" were the same as giving up judgement. So we state vague guesses in complete-sounding sentences, because completeness is reassuring.

But not knowing is not a solid block of black. It comes apart into parts.

You might know that something happened without knowing why. You might know that two things always show up together without knowing whether one causes the other. You might know the cause and still not know what to do next. You might not yet have settled what you want. Each of those calls for a different move. Short of data, go and observe. Short of a model, compare explanations. If values are in conflict, admit the trade-off. If the goal is unclear, stop optimising for a while.

I have come to prefer thinking of the unknown as blank regions on a map rather than as fog. Fog makes it feel as though nothing is visible. A blank region tells you something more useful: this part has not been surveyed, and the rest of the map has not disappeared because of it.

A reliable judgement usually does not take the shape of "I'm sure" or "I'm not sure." It looks more like this. I currently lean towards A, for three reasons; the second reason is the weakest of them; if X shows up tomorrow, I will drop my confidence in A sharply.

That has less force than "this is just how it is," and it is much closer to a working state of knowledge, because it reports two things at once: how I think now, and how I will change.

人對未知有一種奇怪的恐懼。好像承認「我不知道」就等於放棄判斷。於是我們把模糊的推測講得很完整，因為完整感讓人安心。

可是「不知道」並不是一片黑。它可以拆得很細。

你可能知道事情發生了，卻不知道原因；知道兩件事總是一起出現，卻不知道其中有沒有因果；知道原因，卻不知道接下來該做什麼；甚至可能連自己想要的是什麼都還沒決定。這幾種未知需要的動作完全不同。缺資料就去觀察，缺模型就去比較解釋，價值打架就承認取捨，目標不清楚就先別急著優化。

我後來越來越喜歡把未知想成地圖上的空白區，而不是霧。霧讓人覺得什麼都看不見；空白區會提醒你：這一塊還沒測量，其他地方並沒有因此消失。

一個可靠的判斷通常不長成「我確定」或「我不確定」這兩種樣子。它比較像這樣：我目前傾向 A，有三個理由；其中第二個理由最脆弱；如果明天出現 X，我會大幅降低對 A 的信心。

這種說法沒有「事情就是這樣」那麼有力氣，卻更接近真的能工作的認知。因為它同時交代了兩件事：我現在怎麼想，以及我未來會怎麼改。

Understanding an idea and believing it are two different moves

理解一套思想，跟相信它，是兩個動作

Once observation and explanation come apart, another confusion surfaces.

Plenty of people will not properly understand a position they oppose, because they are afraid that understanding amounts to conceding. Religion, politics, and close relationships make this especially visible. We hear a premise we dislike and go straight into rebuttal, and what we end up rebutting is the version in our own head that happened to be easiest to hit.

You can perfectly well understand how a religious teaching handles death and suffering without committing to its metaphysics. You can understand the assumptions under which an economic model holds without believing that people always behave the way the model says. You can understand how somebody's anger was built and still refuse to accept his using it to hurt people.

Understanding is closer to building a simulator that runs. If you genuinely understand a position, you should be able to predict how it answers a situation it has not met, rather than reciting its current slogans. Believing is a separate act: how much truth, value, and commitment to action you are willing to stake on that simulator.

Separate the two and the world of ideas suddenly gets bigger, because you no longer have to decide which side you are on before you are allowed to go in and look.

把觀察和解釋拆開之後，另一個混淆也會浮出水面。

很多人不願意真正理解自己反對的東西，因為他擔心理解等於讓步。宗教、政治、親密關係裡特別明顯。我們一聽見不喜歡的前提，立刻進入反駁模式；結果反駁到的，常常只是自己腦中那個比較好打的版本。

其實你完全可以理解一套宗教教義如何處理死亡與苦難，而不承諾它的形上學主張；可以理解一套經濟模型在什麼假設下有效，而不相信人永遠照模型行動；也可以理解一個人的憤怒是怎麼長出來的，同時不同意他用憤怒傷害別人。

理解比較像替對方裝一台可以運轉的模擬器。當你真的理解一個觀點，你應該能預測它在新情境下會怎麼回答，而不是只會背它現在的口號。相信是另一件事：你願意把多少真實性、價值和行動承諾押在這台模擬器上。

把這兩件事分開之後，思想世界會突然變大。因為你不必先決定「我要不要站在這邊」，才允許自己進去看看。

Back to those three minutes

回到那三分鐘

If we walk back into the meeting at three minutes past ten, things get duller and more workable.

"It started at 10:03" can be confirmed. "The previous meeting ran late" can be checked in the group chat. "No discipline" needs somebody to say which behaviours count as discipline, and whether this is a repeating pattern. "Everyone is strung tight" needs more signal, and might be one colleague's experience of the last few weeks.

Taking those apart does not guarantee the argument ends. At least everybody knows what is being argued about.

This is the first habit in the book. We do not need to get rid of explanation. We need explanation to stay visible. People will always tell stories, and that will not change. What can change is whether we remember we are telling one.

如果我們重新走回十點零三分那場會議，事情會變得比較無聊，也比較可以處理。

「十點零三分開始」可以確認。「上一場會延誤」可以翻群組訊息。「沒有紀律」需要先定義什麼行為算紀律，還要看它是不是重複出現的模式。「大家繃得很緊」需要更多訊號，也可能只是雅琪自己這幾週的感受。

這些東西被拆開之後，爭論不一定會消失。但至少大家知道現在在爭什麼。

這是全書第一個習慣。我們不需要消滅解釋，我們需要讓解釋重新看得見。人永遠會講故事，這件事改不了；能改的是，我們還記不記得自己正在講故事。

So can observation really be separated from explanation?

那麼，觀察真的能跟解釋分開嗎？

A strong objection arrives here. You keep telling people to pull observation apart from explanation, and yet even seeing carries concepts. Without language, without prior knowledge, a person does not know what to attend to. So is pure observation not simply nonexistent?

Half of that objection I accept completely.

I do not believe we can get back to a view from nowhere, with no model in it. Instruments are designed around questions. Data is collected against variables. Attention selects by nature. We cannot even say "there is a cup on the table" without using concepts; table and cup were categories before we opened our mouths.

Still, "there is no pure observation" and "observation and explanation do not differ" are two different sentences.

We can compare how many layers of processing there are, and how far back we can trace them. Camera footage is not the world, and it usually preserves more that two people can check together than "his attitude was bad" does. Raw sensor data is not unmediated reality either, and it is closer to a source that can be reanalysed than the classification derived from it. No map is the territory, and that does not stop us distinguishing satellite imagery from a transit diagram from a tourist illustration.

So what I want is not a return to pure fact. What I want is for the chain of conversions to stay visible. Where did this data come from? Who chose the variables? At which step did classification enter? At which step did causality? And at which step did value slip in?

As long as the chain stays visible, we have one more place to make a correction.

到這裡會出現一個很有力的反駁：你一直叫人把觀察和解釋拆開，可我們連「看見」本身都帶著概念。沒有語言、沒有既有知識，人根本不知道該注意什麼。所謂純粹觀察，是不是根本不存在？

這個反駁有一半我完全同意。

我不相信人能回到一個沒有模型的神之視角。儀器是為了問題設計的，資料是依變數收集的，注意力天生就會挑東西。我們甚至沒辦法在不使用概念的情況下說出「桌上有一只杯子」——「桌」和「杯子」早就是分類了。

不過「沒有純觀察」和「觀察與解釋沒有差別」是兩句不同的話。

我們仍然可以比較加工的層數和可追溯性。攝影機畫面當然不是世界本身，但它通常比「他態度很差」保留了更多可以共同檢查的資訊；原始感測器資料也不是無中介的現實，可它比後續的分類結果更接近一個能重新分析的來源。就像沒有一張地圖等於土地，這也不妨礙我們區分衛星影像、捷運路線圖和旅遊插畫。

所以我想要的東西不是「回到純事實」。我想要的是讓轉換鏈看得見：這筆資料怎麼來的？誰選了變數？哪一步加入分類？哪一步加入因果？哪一步又偷偷加入了價值？

只要鏈條看得見，我們就多了一個修正的入口。

A slow sentence pattern, useful at the moments that count

In a high-conflict situation, reminding everybody not to be subjective achieves almost nothing. Changing the sentence pattern works better.

Instead of "he simply does not respect me," try: he cut me off twice and did not respond to the risk I raised; I am reading those two behaviours as disrespect, though I do not yet know what he was thinking at the time.

Instead of "customers have no need for this feature," try: none of the seven interviewees brought it up unprompted, which lowers my estimate of how strongly it is wanted, though the sample and the way I asked could both be shaping that.

Sentences like these are too slow for ordinary conversation. Their job is to take the steps that were folded together in your head and lay them out once, at a moment that matters.

一個很慢、但在重要時刻有用的句型

在高衝突的場合，一直提醒大家「不要主觀」幾乎沒有用。比較有用的是換一個句型。

把「他就是不尊重我」改成：「他剛才打斷我兩次，也沒有回應我提的風險；我把這兩個行為解釋成不尊重，不過我還不知道他當時在想什麼。」

把「客戶根本不需要這個功能」改成：「目前七位受訪者都沒有主動提到它，這讓我把需求強度往下調；不過樣本和提問方式都可能影響這個結果。」

這種句子太慢，不適合出現在每一段對話裡。它的功能是在重要時刻，把腦中原本折疊起來的步驟重新攤開一次。

Tetlock's hundred thousand forecasts

泰特洛克的十萬個預測

Once you have admitted the unknown, a harder question follows. How sure should I actually be?

Attaching "possibly, perhaps, not necessarily" to every sentence looks humble and can be a way of dodging commitment. Sounding certain does not mean you understand more, either. The difficult part is getting confidence to match evidence.

The psychologist Philip Tetlock spent twenty years doing something plodding and rather remarkable. From the mid-1980s he recruited nearly three hundred people who made their living from judgement — political scientists, regional specialists, intelligence analysts, economic advisers — and asked them to make forecasts on concrete questions that could be scored. Would a particular regime fall within five years. Would a country join a particular organisation. Would an indicator cross a threshold. He required each person to attach a probability, then waited for time to pass and marked the answers one by one. The total ran past eighty thousand.

The results were not flattering. Taken as a whole, the group did only slightly better than chance, and on some question types they did worse than a simple statistical rule that extrapolated from the recent past. One finding deserves more attention than the headline: the more often somebody appeared on television, and the more confident their manner, the lower their accuracy tended to be. They were not more ignorant. They were taking one explanatory tool past the edge of its range and not stopping.

What Tetlock was really measuring is called calibration, and it has little to do with how clever anybody is. If a person says "I'm ninety per cent sure" and, over the long run, is right about ninety per cent of the time, their confidence carries information. Somebody who says ninety per cent regardless of the situation is producing tone of voice, and gets a few right by luck.

Engineering and risk management have thought this way for a long time. Safety factors, confidence intervals, and fault tolerance all treat "how far my knowledge reaches" as decision data in its own right. Everyday judgement is no different. For something that costs ten minutes if you are wrong, thirty per cent confidence may be enough to try. For an irreversible harm, ninety per cent may not be enough. Confidence cannot be discussed apart from cost.

That turns "I don't know" from a question about knowledge into a question about responsibility. Being responsible cannot be explained as guaranteeing that you are always right. It is closer to something else: making a defensible choice when information is limited, and giving errors a chance to be spotted early.

承認未知之後，還有一個更棘手的問題：那我到底該有多大把握？

如果每句話都加上「可能、也許、不一定」，看起來很謙虛，實際上可能只是在逃避承諾。反過來，講得很肯定也不代表真的比較懂。困難的地方在於讓信心和證據對得上。

心理學家菲利普・泰特洛克花了二十年做一件很笨、也很了不起的事。從一九八〇年代中期開始，他找來將近三百位以判斷維生的專業人士——政治學者、區域專家、情報分析員、經濟顧問——請他們對具體問題做出可以打分的預測：某個政權五年內會不會垮、某國會不會加入某個組織、某項指標會不會超過門檻。他要求每個人替自己的預測標上機率，然後等時間過去，一筆一筆對答案。累積下來超過八萬筆。

結果很難看。整體而言，這群人的表現只比隨機猜測好一點；在某些題型上，比一條簡單的統計外推規則還差。更值得注意的是另一件事：越常上電視、講話越有架式的專家，準確度往往更低。他們並沒有比較無知，他們是把一套解釋工具用到超出它的範圍，而且沒有停下來。

泰特洛克想量的東西叫校準，跟聰不聰明關係不大。一個人如果每次說「我有九成把握」的事情，長期下來大約九成成立，那他的信心帶著資訊。另一個人不管什麼情況都說九成，偶爾猜對也只是語氣強。

工程和風險管理早就習慣這樣思考。安全係數、信賴區間、容錯設計，都是把「我知道到哪裡」當成決策資料的做法。日常判斷也一樣。一件錯了只損失十分鐘的事，三成把握就值得試；一件不可逆的傷害，九成把握也可能不夠。信心沒辦法脫離代價單獨談。

這讓「我不知道」從一個認識論問題變成責任問題。負責任沒辦法解釋成「保證自己永遠對」。它比較接近另一件事：在資訊有限的時候做出一個可以辯護的選擇，並且讓錯誤有機會被早一點看見。

Provisional commitment

I have grown fond of the phrase provisional commitment. It is nothing like "I'm not sure, so let's not act." It runs roughly this way. Given what I know now, I am going with A. If A holds, this is the cheaper path. I will be watching X and Y. If X crosses a threshold, I switch to B.

That formulation ties judgement, action, monitoring, and revision into one sentence. It also has a practical effect between people. When a conclusion has been stated as "this is the fact," changing it gets experienced as losing face. When a conclusion was a working assumption from the start, revising it on new data is just normal operation.

Humility does not mean keeping your voice down. Humility means giving your own degree of certainty some structure.

暫時承諾

我很喜歡「暫時承諾」這個講法。它跟「我不確定，所以先不要做」完全不同，長相大概是：依照現在的資訊，我先採用 A；如果 A 成立，這是成本比較低的一條路；我會盯著 X 和 Y；如果 X 超過某個門檻，我就切到 B。

這種寫法把判斷、行動、監測和更新綁在同一句話裡。它還有一個很實際的人際效果。當結論被說成「這就是事實」，改變它會被體驗成丟臉；當結論從一開始就是「目前的工作假設」，新資料出現時，更新就只是正常操作。

謙遜的意思，並不是一直把音量放小。謙遜是讓自己的確定程度長出結構。

2 — One Cup, Four Answers

第二章　同一只杯子，四種答案

The same thing admits many correct descriptions, because "important" never exists apart from a purpose.

同一個東西可以有很多種正確的描述，因為「重要」這兩個字從來不會脫離目的而存在。

There is a cup on the table.

If I ask you what it is, the answer is too easy. A cup.

Bring a few other people in and the answers start to diverge. The mover who walks in sees a fragile item before he sees a cup, and what he cares about is size, weight, and whether it stacks. The product designer looks at the angle of the handle, the thickness of the rim, whether the tooling came out cleanly. The cleaner notices whether the groove around the base will trap residue. The forensics examiner may not care at all whether it holds water; he wants to know whether there are prints on it, what the traces are, and roughly when they were left.

Which of these is the cup's real nature?

The question sounds like a philosophy exam, and it causes trouble every day in companies, families, and technical systems. We are in the habit of hiding the question we are answering, and then arguing fiercely about the answer.

桌上有一只杯子。

我問你「這是什麼」，答案太簡單了：杯子。

可是換幾個人進來，答案就開始分岔。搬家公司的師傅走進來，第一眼看到的是一件易碎物，他關心的是尺寸、重量、能不能疊。產品設計師看的是握把的角度、杯緣的厚度、模具開得漂不漂亮。清潔人員注意杯底那圈溝槽會不會積垢。鑑識人員可能完全不在乎它能不能裝水，他只想知道杯身上有沒有指紋、殘留物是什麼、留下的時間大概多久。

哪一個才是這只杯子「真正的樣子」？

這個問題聽起來像哲學系的期末考，可它每天都在公司、家庭和技術系統裡製造麻煩。我們習慣把自己正在回答的問題藏起來，然後為答案吵得很兇。

There is a question hidden inside the word "important"

「重要」這兩個字裡面藏著一個問題

Any act of understanding has to throw something away. This has nothing to do with laziness. If nothing is discarded, understanding never takes shape.

A map that drew every speck of dust in a city would be harder to use than the city. A financial statement does not record every conversation in the office. A health check does not measure every molecule in a body. Our judgement of a friend cannot possibly retain his entire history from birth. A model is a form of selective forgetting.

So what should be forgotten? The answer is not "whatever is least important," because importance itself depends on what you are trying to do.

任何理解都必須丟掉東西。這件事和偷懶無關；如果什麼都不丟，理解根本無法成形。

一張把城市裡每一粒灰塵都畫出來的地圖，會比城市本身更難使用。財務報表不會記錄辦公室裡的每一場對話，健康檢查不會測量人體的每一個分子，我們對一個朋友的判斷也不可能保留他從出生到現在的全部歷史。所謂模型，就是一種有選擇的遺忘。

那該忘掉什麼？答案並不是「越不重要的越先忘」。因為重要與否本身就取決於你要做什麼。

For drinking, capacity and material matter. For logistics, weight and stackability matter. For archaeology, the period and the marks of manufacture matter. Purpose is not a condition bolted on after the model is finished. From the first second, it is deciding what gets into the model at all.

This is why a lot of large questions are asked wrongly from the start. "Which management method is best?" has almost no answerable content without organisation size, talent structure, time horizon, and the cost of failure. "Does AI have intelligence?" turns easily into a fight over nouns unless somebody first says which capability we want to predict, in what environment, and what kind of failure is tolerable.

The bigger the question, the more it needs its purpose brought up onto the table first.

對喝水來說，容量和材質重要；對物流來說，重量和堆疊性重要；對考古來說，年代和製作痕跡重要。目的並不是模型做完之後再附加上去的一個條件，它從第一秒就在決定什麼東西進得了模型。

這也是為什麼很多大問題一開始就問錯了。「哪一種管理方法最好？」少了組織規模、人才結構、時間尺度和失敗成本，這句話幾乎沒有可回答的內容。「AI 有沒有智慧？」如果不先說我們想預測哪種能力、在什麼環境、容許什麼樣的失敗，討論很容易只剩下搶名詞。

問題越大，越需要先把目的搬到桌面上。

Expertise is a discipline of ignoring

專業是一套有紀律的忽略

A doctor, an engineer, a lawyer, an accountant, and a designer looking at the same situation will notice different differences. This does not mean one of them is closer to the world. Each profession has trained a set of rules about what can be left unexamined for now.

Those rules are powerful. They let an expert handle in minutes what looks like chaos to a beginner.

Professional blind spots grow out of the same place: the problem changes and the rules about what to ignore do not.

An image recognition model chasing average accuracy in the lab is a reasonable thing. Deploy it on a low-power device and latency, memory footprint, and the cost of a false positive suddenly become the binding constraints. If the team is still using the same leaderboard to decide which model is best, the model has not got worse. The problem changed a while ago and the evaluation is still living in the old one.

Management works the same way. A company says it wants to improve efficiency. Finance hears cost reduction, engineering hears less rework, product hears a shorter cycle from request to user. Everybody agrees efficiency matters, and they are working in four different worlds.

Plenty of arguments never reach a conclusion because they were never arguments about answers. They were arguments about the question.

醫師、工程師、律師、會計師、設計師面對同一件事，會注意到不同的差異。這不代表誰比較接近世界。每一種專業都在訓練一套「什麼可以暫時不看」的規則。

這些規則很有力量。它們讓專家在幾分鐘內處理掉新手眼中的一團混亂。

專業盲點也從同一個地方長出來：問題換了，忽略規則卻沒換。

一套影像辨識模型在實驗室裡追求平均準確率，這很合理。部署到低功耗裝置之後，延遲、記憶體佔用和誤判成本忽然變成主要約束。如果團隊還用同一張排行榜決定「哪個模型最好」，模型並沒有退步；問題早就換了，評估方式卻還活在舊問題裡。

管理也一樣。公司說要「提高效率」，財務理解成降低成本，研發理解成減少重工，產品理解成把從需求到使用者的週期縮短。所有人都同意效率很重要，卻在四個不同的世界裡工作。

很多爭論之所以一直沒有結論，是因為它們根本不是答案之爭。它們是問題之爭。

Purpose has three layers, and the middle one gets skipped

目的有三層，中間那層最常被跳過

"Ask about the purpose first" turns into a management slogan very easily, so it needs digging.

The first layer is the task in front of you: what has to be finished today. The second is what finishing it buys: why it is worth doing. The third is a longer time horizon: whether today's success damages what actually matters in six months.

A project can hit its launch date by accumulating code nobody dares touch. A department can make this quarter's numbers look good by pushing the problem into next quarter. A person can avoid tonight's conflict in a way that costs a relationship its trust three years later. Local purposes are not wrong in themselves. What goes wrong is a local purpose quietly passing itself off as the whole.

So purpose needs auditing too. Who set it? Who benefits? Who carries the cost of what it ignored? Which constraints are not available for trade?

Suppose a customer service policy aims to shorten average call time. It may genuinely make the numbers prettier. If complex problems get transferred away quickly, users have to explain themselves twice, and staff start avoiding the hard cases, then the metric was met and the service got worse. Once a purpose is compressed into an indicator, the proxy starts to displace the thing it was meant to protect.

Purpose is less like a blank to be filled in and more like a tree. Above it are higher reasons. Beside it are constraints that cannot be ignored. Below it are the indicators and methods you have provisionally adopted.

「先問目的」很容易變成一句管理口號，所以要再往下挖。

第一層是眼前的任務：今天要完成什麼。第二層是這個任務要換來什麼：為什麼完成它值得。第三層是更長的時間尺度：今天的成功會不會破壞半年後真正要緊的事。

一個專案可以為了準時上線而累積一堆沒人敢碰的程式碼；一個部門可以為了讓本季 KPI 好看，把問題推到下一季；一個人可以為了避免今天晚上的衝突，讓一段關係在三年之後失去信任。局部目的本身沒有錯，錯的是它在不知不覺之間冒充了整體目的。

所以「目的」本身也需要被審查：誰設定它？誰得到好處？誰承擔被忽略的代價？哪些限制不能拿來交換？

假設一套客服制度的目標是縮短平均通話時間。它可能真的讓數字變漂亮，可是如果複雜問題被快速轉接、使用者需要重複說明、員工開始避開難題，那麼指標完成了，服務反而變差。目的透過指標被壓縮之後，代理物開始取代它原本想保護的東西。

目的因此不像一個填完就結束的空格。它比較像一棵樹：上面有更高階的理由，旁邊有不能忽略的限制，下面有暫時採用的指標和手段。

Switching lenses

換一副鏡頭

We talk about one thing being more abstract and another more concrete, as though abstraction had a fixed staircase. Go back to the cup and it does not work that way.

Seeing the cup as a container is not a higher rung than seeing it as a fragile item. They follow different purposes and keep different differences.

I prefer to think of abstraction as switching lenses. A wide angle shows you the relations across a whole scene, a long lens shows you local detail, infrared brings out temperature differences that were not visible at all. No lens equals the world. A lens is worth something for a specific reason: for the problem in front of me now, which kind of difference does it make visible?

This view has an important consequence. Every act of abstraction creates a blind region at the same time.

When a company compresses employees into performance scores, the comparable differences get clearer, and collaboration, developing other people, and long-term effects may be flattened along with them. When a medical system sorts people into normal and abnormal at a threshold, decisions get faster and individual variation near the boundary gets discretised away. When a vision model represents a person on the street as a rectangle, it gains a very useful visual object and loses that person's story, intentions, and identity.

Abstraction is not the problem. Forgetting what the abstraction did is the problem.

我們常說「這個比較抽象」「那個比較具體」，好像抽象有一座固定的階梯。回到杯子就會發現事情不長這樣。

把杯子看成「容器」並沒有比看成「易碎物」更高階。它們沿著不同的目的，留下不同的差異。

我比較願意把抽象想成換鏡頭。廣角讓你看見整體關係，長焦讓你看見局部細節，紅外線讓原本不可見的溫度差異浮出來。沒有一顆鏡頭等於世界本身。鏡頭的價值在於：對現在這個問題，它讓哪一種差異變得看得見？

這個看法有一個很重要的後果。每一次抽象，都同時創造一個盲區。

公司把員工壓成績效分數，可比較的差異變清楚了，協作、育成和長期影響也可能一起被壓掉。醫療系統把人分進「正常／異常」兩邊，決策變快了，邊界附近的個體差異則被離散化。當 AI 把街上的行人表示成一個個矩形框，它得到一個非常好用的視覺物件，同時失去那個人的故事、意圖和身分。

抽象本身沒有問題。忘記抽象做過什麼，才是問題。

A clumsier question that holds up better

一個比較笨、但比較可靠的問法

The next time you meet "which is better," "does this even count," or "what is the essential nature of this," you can decline to answer and rewrite it into something clumsier:

下次遇到「哪個比較好」「這到底算不算」「本質是什麼」這類大問題，可以先不回答，把它改寫成一句比較笨的話：

For what purpose, under which conditions and over what time horizon, do I need to keep which differences, in order to support which action?
為了什麼目的，在什麼條件和時間尺度下，我需要留住哪些差異，才能支持什麼行動？

That sentence has none of the elegance of a philosophical slogan, and it smells faintly of engineering. Its use is to force a vague question to grow coordinates. Once coordinates appear, a lot of arguments that looked like arguments about the nature of the world show their real shape: we are choosing a way of looking.

這句話沒有哲學口號漂亮，甚至有點工程味。它的用處是逼一個模糊的問題長出座標。而只要座標出現，很多原本看起來在爭世界本質的討論，就會露出真正的形狀：我們其實在挑一種看世界的方法。

Who gets to decide what we are solving

誰有權決定「我們現在要解決什麼」

If purpose analysis only ever reaches "ask about the goal first," it turns into a tool for making existing power more efficient.

A company says the goal is lower cost, so the algorithm lowers cost. A government says the goal is better traffic throughput, so the system improves throughput. Technically this can be entirely correct, and three questions have been skipped. Why does this goal get to override the others? Who took part in defining it? Who carries the part of the cost that never entered the model?

New York in the 1960s offers a very clear case. Robert Moses, at that point the most powerful planner in America, controlled enormous public works budgets, and his question was precise: how do you make cars move through a city more freely. That goal was not sinister. Post-war America almost universally agreed that cars meant progress. Working from it, Moses built expressways across New York and demolished the neighbourhoods along their routes. In the early sixties he proposed a road that would cut straight across Lower Manhattan, through what is now SoHo and Little Italy.

Among the people who opposed it was a writer living in Greenwich Village named Jane Jacobs. Her 1961 book, The Death and Life of Great American Cities, did something that amounts to redescribing the same street under a different purpose. Moses's question was traffic flow. Jacobs's question was how a street stays safe and alive. Under her lens, the shopkeeper glancing up from the counter all day is a security system, and short blocks with mixed uses are an economic system. Neither of those has a field in a traffic model. The expressway was finally killed in 1969.

What that fight was about was not whose data was more accurate. Both sides could probably do their sums. They were fighting over who got to decide which problem the city was solving.

Organisations work the same way. A purpose is rarely just a variable in somebody's head. It is usually an outcome of power. So I tend to split purpose into three layers. The task purpose answers what has to be done now. The system purpose answers why that is worth doing. The legitimacy condition asks which costs should not be decided by one party alone, even when the trade would buy efficiency.

The third layer is what stops "ask about the purpose" from sliding into pure optimisation.

目的分析如果只做到「先問目標」，很容易變成一個替既有權力提高效率的工具。

公司說目標是降低成本，演算法就去降低成本；政府說目標是提高通行效率，系統就去提高通行效率。技術上完全正確，被跳過的是另外三個問題：為什麼這個目標可以壓過其他目標？誰參與了定義？誰承擔它沒放進模型的那部分代價？

一九六〇年代的紐約有一個很清楚的例子。當時全美最有權力的都市規劃者羅伯・摩斯手上握著大量公共工程資源，他的問題非常明確：怎麼讓汽車在城市裡跑得更順。這個目標並不邪惡，戰後的美國幾乎所有人都同意汽車代表進步。摩斯依照這個目標，在紐約蓋了大量快速道路，也拆掉了沿線的社區。到了六〇年代初，他提出一條要橫穿下曼哈頓的高速公路，路線經過的正是今天的蘇活區和小義大利。

反對它的人裡面，有一位住在格林威治村的作家珍・雅各。她在一九六一年出版了《美國大城市的死與生》，書裡做的事情，本質上就是換一個目的重新描述同一條街道。摩斯的問題是「車流」，雅各的問題是「一條街怎麼保持安全和活力」。在雅各的鏡頭下，路邊雜貨店老闆一整天不經意的張望是一套治安系統，短街廓和混合用途是一套經濟系統——這些東西在車流模型裡完全沒有欄位。那條高速公路最後在一九六九年被擋下來。

這場衝突真正的內容並不是「誰的數據比較準」。兩邊的計算大概都沒有錯。他們爭的是誰有權決定這座城市現在要解決什麼問題。

在組織裡也一樣。目的很少只是某個人腦中的變數，它通常是權力的結果。所以我傾向把目的拆成三層：任務目的回答眼前要做什麼；系統目的回答它為何值得；正當性條件則問，哪些代價即使能換來效率，也不該由某一方單獨決定。

第三層讓「先問目的」不至於滑成純粹的最佳化。

Wald's bullet holes

沃德的彈孔

A purpose can be met beautifully and still be the wrong problem.

During the Second World War the American military faced a practical difficulty: bomber losses were too high, and armour had to go somewhere. Armour is heavy, and a plane carrying too much of it cannot fly, so the placement had to be chosen. They did the apparently sensible thing and counted the bullet holes in the aircraft that came back, looking for the areas with the densest damage so they could reinforce them.

At Columbia there was a unit called the Statistical Research Group, and in it a mathematician named Abraham Wald. He pointed out a structural problem with the data. Every aircraft in the sample was an aircraft that had returned. Holes clustering in certain areas might simply mean that a hit there still let you fly home, while the genuinely fatal locations brought planes down where nobody counted them. Armour, on that reading, belonged where the returning aircraft showed the fewest holes.

Wald's actual work was far more careful than the popular version — he developed a method for estimating vulnerability from surviving samples — and the core of the story is not exaggerated. The military had asked where the holes were. Wald changed the question to which hits stop you coming back. Same data, one substitution, and the answer inverts.

This is why I think redefining a problem is a higher-order skill than finding a better answer. Many significant breakthroughs did not come from finally finishing off the original problem. Somebody noticed that we had been treating something variable as fixed, treating an unimportant difference as important, treating a proxy as the goal.

Abstraction does more than subtract; it can also discover. Some problems are hard because we have been using the wrong representation the whole time, and not because the data is thin. Turn a discrete classification into a continuous quantity, turn an individual problem into a process problem, turn "whose fault is this" into "which feedback loop got slower," and the structure of the situation can suddenly become workable.

A team that keeps investigating which person is inefficient will improve only so far. Restate the problem as waiting time, dependency, and rework loops, and a question about personalities becomes a question about a system.

This is not word games. The representation decides which kind of causality you are able to see.

一個目的可以被漂亮地達成，同時仍然是錯的問題。

第二次世界大戰期間，美軍面對一個很實際的難題：轟炸機損失太高，該在哪裡加裝甲？裝甲很重，加太多飛不動，所以必須挑地方。軍方做了看起來最合理的事：統計返航飛機上的彈孔分布，找出哪些部位彈孔最密，然後在那些地方加厚。

哥倫比亞大學有一個叫「統計研究組」的單位，裡面有位數學家亞伯拉罕・沃德。他指出這份資料有一個結構性的問題：能被統計到的飛機，全都是飛回來的飛機。彈孔集中在某些部位，可能只是因為打在那些部位還能撐著回家；而那些真正致命的位置，飛機當場就掉下去了，永遠不會出現在統計表上。所以裝甲應該加在返航飛機上彈孔最少的地方。

沃德的實際工作比這個流行版本細緻得多，他寫的是一整套從倖存樣本推估被擊落機率的方法。但故事的核心沒有被誇大：軍方原本問的是「彈孔在哪裡」，沃德把它改成「哪些位置被打中就回不來」。同一批資料，換一次問題，答案整個翻過來。

我因此認為「重新定義問題」比「找到更好的答案」是更高階的能力。很多重大突破的起點，是有人發現我們一直把不該固定的東西當成固定，把不重要的差異當成重要，把代理指標當成目的；原本那個問題根本沒有被解完。

抽象除了刪減，也能發現。有些問題很難，難在我們一直用錯表示，跟資料多寡關係不大。把離散分類改成連續量，把個體問題改成流程問題，把「這是誰的錯」改成「哪一段回饋延遲了」，世界的結構可能突然變得可以處理。

一個團隊如果一直在追究「哪個人效率差」，怎麼改善都很有限；一旦把問題換成工作等待時間、依賴關係和重工循環，原本的人格問題就變成系統問題。

這不是語言遊戲。表示方式會決定你能看見哪一種因果。

Who pays for the simplification

誰替這個簡化付錢

Every abstraction makes some differences disappear. That in itself carries no moral weight. The awkward part is that a disappeared difference sometimes turns into somebody else's cost.

A credit score compresses a complicated life into a risk number, which is extremely convenient for a financial system, and the person sitting near the boundary may lose an opportunity because of it. A company compresses performance into quantifiable indicators, management gets easier, and the employees who do the collaborating, the mentoring, the firefighting, and the long-term groundwork can become invisible.

So an abstraction audit needs a third question alongside "what was kept" and "what was discarded": who pays for this simplification?

That question matters especially because the beneficiaries of an abstraction and the people carrying its costs are often not the same group. The person who designs the form gets consistency; the person filling it in absorbs the loss of context. The system gets efficiency; the boundary cases absorb the misclassifications. When an abstraction is one person's private notebook, the cost is limited. When it becomes an institutional interface, the ethical weight goes up.

每一種抽象都會讓一些差異消失。這件事本身沒有道德好壞，麻煩的是被消失的差異有時候會變成別人的代價。

一套信用評分把複雜的人生壓成一個風險分數，對金融系統非常方便；落在邊界上的那個人可能因此失去機會。公司把績效壓成可量化指標，管理變容易了；那些做協作、帶新人、救火和長期基礎工作的員工可能整個變成隱形。

所以抽象審計除了問「留下什麼、捨棄什麼」，還要問第三件事：誰替這個簡化付錢？

這個問題特別重要，因為抽象的受益者和代價承擔者常常不是同一群人。設計表格的人得到一致性，填表的人承擔脈絡被壓掉。系統得到效率，邊界個案承擔誤判。當抽象只是一個人的私人筆記，代價有限；當抽象變成制度的接口，倫理責任就提高了。

3 — The Tube Map That Got It Wrong

第三章　那張畫錯的地鐵圖

A model's trouble was never that it is incomplete. The trouble is what it left out so thoroughly that we can no longer see it.

模型的麻煩從來不是它不完整。麻煩在於它把某些東西省略到我們再也看不見。

In 1931 a draughtsman at the London Underground named Harry Beck was out of work, his post cut in a round of downsizing. At home he took a sheet of paper and did something that looked absurd at the time: he threw away the geographic scale of the Underground network.

The maps before his were drawn to real geography. Central London's stations crowded into an unreadable knot while the suburban lines stretched out long and empty. Beck's day job was drawing circuit diagrams, and it occurred to him that a passenger underground has no use for geography. A passenger needs three things: which stations a line passes, where you can change, and which direction to board.

So he pulled every line into horizontals, verticals, and forty-five degree diagonals, enlarged the centre, compressed the outskirts, coded the lines by colour, and let the Thames be the only geographic object left on the sheet. Almost every station on that map sits in the wrong place.

The publicity department turned it down the first time as too radical. Two years later they printed a small trial folder, and Beck is said to have been paid five guineas for it. Passengers responded so well that the company had to reprint immediately. Ninety years on, transit systems worldwide are speaking the same visual language.

If you land in Tokyo for the first time and are handed a subway map, you are unlikely to complain that it is not to scale. Some stations look close and are a twenty-minute walk apart; rivers, gradients, and street detail barely exist. It is plainly distorted and it works beautifully. A map drawn to exact scale, dense with terrain, would help you less with changing trains.

There is an important turn buried in that small piece of history. A model's usefulness often comes from its willingness to stop resembling the world.

一九三一年，倫敦地鐵公司有一位叫哈利・貝克的製圖員，那時他因為公司縮編正處於待業狀態。他在家裡拿出一張紙，做了一件在當時看起來很離譜的事：他把倫敦地鐵路線圖上的地理比例全部丟掉。

在他之前的地鐵圖是照著真實地理畫的。倫敦市中心的車站密密麻麻擠成一團，郊區的路線則拉得又長又空，整張圖幾乎沒辦法看。貝克平常畫的是電路圖，他想到，搭地鐵的人在地底下根本不需要知道地理。乘客只需要知道三件事：這條線經過哪些站、哪裡可以換車、往哪個方向搭。

於是他把所有路線拉成水平、垂直和四十五度的直線，把市中心放大、郊區壓縮，用顏色區分路線，並且讓泰晤士河成為圖上唯一保留的地理物件。這張圖上幾乎每一個站的位置都是錯的。

公司的宣傳部門第一次看到它的時候拒絕了，理由是太激進。兩年後他們才勉強印了一批小折頁試水溫，據說付給貝克五個金幣。結果乘客反應好到公司必須立刻加印。九十年後，全世界的大眾運輸系統幾乎都在用同一套語言。

如果你第一次到東京，拿到一張地鐵路線圖，你大概不會抱怨它沒有按照真實比例。某些站看起來很近，實際走路要二十分鐘；河流、坡度、街區細節幾乎不存在。它明明失真，卻很好用。反過來，一張比例精確、標滿地形細節的地圖，對轉乘這件事幫助反而更小。

這件小事包含一個很重要的認知轉折：模型的用處經常來自它敢於不像世界。

Compression is what makes a map usable

壓縮讓地圖變得能用

We tend to treat simplification as a compromise forced on us, as though the ideal model would retain as much reality as possible. Something that genuinely retained every detail would no longer be a model. It would be a second copy of the world, equally hard to handle.

Models have to compress. The only question is how.

A weather forecast turns the state of the atmosphere into a handful of variables and probabilities. A neural network compresses regularities in a mass of data into parameters. A person's understanding of a colleague compresses a few hundred interactions into "he goes conservative under pressure." None of these is reality, and each of them makes prediction and action possible.

In late August 1854, cholera broke out in Soho and killed more than five hundred people in ten days. The prevailing view was that cholera travelled through bad air. A physician practising nearby, John Snow, was unconvinced, and he did something very simple: he took a street map, marked each death as a small stroke, and marked the locations of the public water pumps.

That drawing has no miasma on it, no wind direction, no smell, and nothing about the occupations or the moral character of the victims — all of which were considered highly relevant at the time. Two kinds of information survived: where people died, and where the water was. The marks clustered densely around the pump on Broad Street. Snow took the map to the local board of governors, and on 8 September the handle was removed.

Snow could not prove the cause at that point — the bacterium was not confirmed for another thirty years — and later research indicates the outbreak was already declining before the handle came off. What makes that drawing remarkable is not what it proved. It is that he chose the right two variables to keep. Represent an epidemic as death-points plus water-points and a disaster with no visible structure becomes something you can act on.

我們習慣把「簡化」當成不得已的妥協，好像理想模型應該盡量多留一點現實。可是一個真的把所有細節都留下來的東西，已經不算模型了，它只是另一份同樣難處理的世界。

模型必須壓縮。問題只在於怎麼壓。

天氣預報把大氣狀態轉成少數變數和機率；神經網路把大量資料裡的規律壓進參數；一個人對同事的理解，會把幾百次互動壓成一句「他在壓力下會先保守」。這些壓縮都不是現實本身，但它們讓預測和行動變成可能。

一八五四年八月底，倫敦蘇活區爆發霍亂，十天之內死了五百多人。當時主流的看法是霍亂透過空氣中的「瘴氣」傳播。一位在附近開業的醫師約翰・史諾不太相信，他做了一件很簡單的事：拿一張街道圖，把每一個死亡案例標成一個小記號，再標出附近所有公共水泵的位置。

那張圖上沒有瘴氣，沒有風向，沒有氣味，也沒有病人的職業和道德品行——這些在當時被認為關係重大的東西全部被丟掉了。留下來的只有兩種資訊：死在哪裡、水泵在哪裡。記號密密麻麻地圍著布洛德街那口水泵。史諾拿著這張圖去說服地方委員會，九月八日，那口水泵的把手被拆掉了。

史諾當時還沒有辦法證明病因（霍亂弧菌要到三十年後才被確認），而且後來的研究也指出疫情在拆把手之前就已經開始下降。這張圖厲害的地方在於它選對了要留下的兩個變數。同一場疫情，一旦被表示成「死亡點」加「水源點」，一個原本看不出結構的災難就變得可以行動。

So when somebody says a model is not reality, the sentence has not yet done any work. Of course it is not. The question with more information in it: which relations did this model keep? Is its distortion purposeful or unnoticed? And which costs did it move somewhere out of sight?

所以當有人說「模型不是真實」的時候，這句話本身還不夠。當然不是真實。更有資訊量的問題是：這個模型留下了哪些關係？它的失真是有目的的，還是無意識的？它把什麼代價搬到看不見的地方去了？

Complexity does not vanish, it relocates

複雜度沒有消失，它只是搬家

Modern life leans heavily on things that look simple. You press a phone and half an hour later food arrives at the door. You call an API and a few lines of code make use of an enormously complicated system behind it. You glance at a green light on a dashboard and know things are normal.

Those simplifications are real. For the user, the world genuinely did get simpler.

The complexity did not disappear. It usually moves: to the platform backend, the operations team, the exception handling, the data cleaning, the support desk, the regulators, the supply chain, or onto some group of people the system boundary excluded.

This is why many systems look elegant in ordinary times and then, when something breaks, suddenly nobody knows how to repair them. Encapsulation hid the complexity so well that even its location was forgotten.

Engineering talks about technical debt. Plenty of concepts accumulate something similar, an abstraction debt: what was omitted for the sake of simplicity becomes important again after the environment shifts, and the organisation has forgotten it was ever omitted.

A model evaluation that looks only at average accuracy works well while the data is stable. Change the camera, the image pipeline, or the user population, and the distribution differences that were averaged away become the main problem. The team's instinct at that point is to tune the model again, and the debt they actually owe may not be in the parameters. It may be that the original representation left the environment out.

現代生活大量依賴那些「看起來很簡單」的東西。你按一下手機，三十分鐘後食物送到門口；你呼叫一個 API，幾行程式就使用了背後極其複雜的系統；你看一眼儀表板上的綠燈，就知道「目前正常」。

這些簡化是真的。對使用者來說，世界確實變簡單了。

只是複雜度沒有憑空消失。它通常被搬到別的地方：平台後端、維運團隊、例外處理、資料清理、客服、法規、供應鏈，或者某些被系統邊界排除在外的人身上。

這也是很多系統在平常看起來極其優雅、出事時卻忽然沒有人知道怎麼修的原因。封裝把複雜度藏得太成功，最後連「複雜度在哪裡」都被忘掉。

工程界談技術債。其實很多概念也會累積一種「抽象債」：當初為了簡化而省略的東西，在環境改變之後重新變得重要，可是組織已經忘了它曾經被省略。

一套只看平均準確率的模型評估，在資料穩定的時候很好用。攝影機、影像處理晶片、使用族群一換，原本被平均掉的分布差異忽然成為主要問題。這時候團隊的直覺通常是「再調模型」，但欠下的債可能在更前面：當初那套表示把環境條件整個排除在外。

Boundaries are drawn by people and their consequences are real

邊界是人畫的，後果是真的

The moment a model starts compressing, boundaries appear.

Adult and minor. Normal and abnormal. High risk and low risk. Person and non-person. Intelligent and not intelligent. Language and institutions need boundaries, because action cannot stay on a continuous spectrum forever. Law has to pick a day on which somebody becomes an adult. A system has to pick a number above which an alarm fires. Medicine has to pick a point at which further tests are recommended.

The phenomenon itself does not necessarily break there.

That does not make boundaries fictional. It means a boundary usually contains two things at once: an observation about how the world behaves, and a choice made for the sake of acting.

Forget the second and you mistake a cut made for the convenience of deciding for a seam that nature put there. A risk score above seventy is classified as high risk, and the person at sixty-nine and the person at seventy do not become two kinds of being over one point. What exists is a continuous risk and an institutional threshold. The threshold may be entirely reasonable, even necessary. Reasonable is not the same as natural.

Keeping that distinction lets you avoid two extremes at once. On one side, all categories are fictions so none of them matter. On the other, the category exists, therefore nature is built this way.

只要模型開始壓縮，就會產生邊界。

「成年人」和「未成年人」、「正常」和「異常」、「高風險」和「低風險」、「人」和「非人」、「有智慧」和「沒有智慧」。語言和制度需要邊界，因為行動不能永遠停在連續光譜上。法律必須決定哪一天算成年，系統必須決定超過哪個數字觸發警報，醫療必須決定什麼時候建議進一步檢查。

現象本身未必剛好在那裡斷掉。

這不表示邊界都是假的。它表示邊界通常同時包含兩樣東西：對世界規律的觀察，以及為了行動而做的選擇。

當我們忘記第二樣，就會把「為了方便決策而切的一刀」誤認成「世界天然就有一條刀痕」。某項風險分數超過七十就列為高風險，六十九和七十的人不會因為一分之差突然變成兩種存在。真正存在的是一條連續的風險，加上一道制度門檻。門檻可能非常合理，甚至必要；合理並不等於自然。

這個區分讓我們同時避開兩個極端。一邊是「所有分類都是虛構，所以都不用管」；另一邊是「只要分類存在，自然界本來就長這樣」。

A model is more like an interface than a mirror

模型像介面

The metaphor I have come to like most for a model is an interface.

The folder icon on a desktop does not mean there is a yellow paper folder inside the drive. It is an interface: it turns a complicated underlying state into a form a person can operate. An interface does not have to resemble what is underneath. It only has to hold certain operational relations reliably.

Concepts work much the same way. Company, market, personality, disease, intelligence are high-level objects that let us operate on top of enormous complexity. Using them day to day is fine, and without them we could not think at all.

What matters is keeping one capability: when the interface fails, knowing you can look further down.

A senior engineer does not stare at the display because the display is wrong; he knows there are logs, state, memory, network, and hardware underneath. A good user of ideas is the same. In ordinary times you can say he is conservative, this market has matured, this model is good. The moment results diverge from expectations, remember those high-level words are an entrance rather than a destination.

The better a model is, the more transparent it becomes. Once transparent, what we see is no longer the model. It is "the world is just like this."

So the discipline that matters most with a model is remembering it is there, which is more useful than doubting it constantly.

我後來最喜歡用「介面」來理解模型。

電腦桌面上的資料夾圖示，並不代表硬碟裡真的有一個黃色的紙夾。它是一個介面：把底層的複雜狀態轉成適合人操作的形式。介面不必長得像底層，它只要可靠地維持某些操作關係。

概念也很像介面。「公司」「市場」「人格」「疾病」「智慧」都是讓我們能在巨大複雜度上操作的高層物件。平常使用它們完全沒有問題，甚至沒有它們就無法思考。

要緊的是保留一種能力：當介面失效時，知道可以往下看。

資深工程師不會因為畫面顯示錯誤就只盯著畫面，他知道底下還有日誌、狀態、記憶體、網路、硬體。好的思想使用者也一樣。平常可以說「他很保守」「這個市場成熟了」「這個模型很好」，可是一旦結果和預期不一致，就要記得這些高層詞彙是入口，不是終點。

模型越好用，越容易變透明。透明之後，我們看到的就不再是模型，而是「世界本來就是這樣」。

所以對模型最重要的修養是記得它的存在。這比一直懷疑它有用得多。

Korzybski's dog biscuits

柯日布斯基的狗餅乾

"The map is not the territory" comes from a Polish-American scholar, Alfred Korzybski. In Science and Sanity, published in 1933, he built an entire discussion of language and reality on that comparison. A map is useful if its structure is similar to the territory's, and a map is never the territory; the mistake people make most often is taking their own language for the world.

There is a demonstration of his that gets retold frequently. He was making the point that people eat words as well as food, and he took a packet of biscuits out of his bag and offered them to the front row. Students ate them, said they were good, and a couple took a second. When most of the packet was gone he tore off the white paper wrapper to reveal the packaging underneath: dog biscuits. Several students ran out to be sick.

His comment, roughly, was that he had just demonstrated that people do not only eat food, they eat words — and that the nausea words cause can be stronger than the food itself.

The story is crude in exactly the right way. It is not saying labels do nothing; labels do plenty, and those students' reactions are perfectly understandable. It points at something else: a large share of our response to the world is a response to our own label, and we normally cannot detect that layer.

「地圖不是土地」這句話出自一位波蘭裔的美國學者阿爾弗雷德・柯日布斯基。他在一九三三年出版的《科學與健全》裡用這個比喻建立了一整套關於語言與現實的討論：地圖的結構如果和土地相似，它就有用；但地圖永遠不是土地本身，而人最常犯的錯，是把自己的語言當成了世界。

關於他，有一個常被轉述的課堂示範。他在講到「人不只吃食物，也吃語言」的時候，從包裡拿出一包餅乾請前排學生吃。學生吃了，說很好吃，還有人多拿了一片。等大家吃得差不多，他把外面那層白紙撕掉，露出底下的包裝：狗餅乾。有幾個學生立刻衝出去吐。

柯日布斯基的評論大意是：我剛才示範的是，人不只吃食物，也吃字；而字造成的噁心，有時候比食物本身更強烈。

這個故事的粗糙程度剛好。它不是在說標籤沒有作用——標籤當然有作用，而且那些學生的反應完全可以理解。它指出的是另一件事：我們對世界的反應，有很大一部分是對自己那張標籤的反應，而我們通常察覺不到這一層。

The map is not the territory, and the territory will embarrass the map

土地會讓地圖難堪

"The map is not the territory" turns very easily into a breezy relativism: everybody has their own map, so let everybody walk their own way.

I do not accept that step.

There can be many maps, and the territory constrains them in return. You can draw a road that does not exist and the car will not get through. You can write a higher load rating on the bridge and the bridge will not get stronger. A company can switch to a better-looking KPI and the cash will still run out. A person can hold firmly to the belief that a relationship is fine and the other person may still leave.

Feedback that cannot be removed by changing how you talk is what I call a reality constraint. It does not necessarily tell us what the world finally is, and it keeps telling us something: at minimum, you cannot say that.

This is the balance point I think matters most in any view of models. Granting that we reach the world through representations does not mean the world is settled by representation. Models can be plural; outcomes are not equivalent.

Which brings us to a harder question. If a model was never the world, on what basis do we say one model is better?

「地圖不是土地」很容易被說成一種瀟灑的相對主義：既然每個人都有自己的地圖，那就各走各的。

我不接受這一步。

地圖可以有很多張，土地會反過來限制它們。你可以把不存在的路畫上去，車開不過去；可以把橋的承重寫高一點，橋不會因此變強；公司可以換一個更好看的 KPI，現金流照樣會耗盡；一個人可以堅信這段關係很好，對方仍然可能離開。

這種沒辦法靠改說法消除的回饋，我把它叫做「實在約束」。它不見得會告訴我們世界最終是什麼樣子，卻會不斷告訴我們：至少不能隨便這樣說。

這是我認為一套模型觀最重要的平衡點。承認我們透過表示接近世界，並不等於世界由表示任意決定。模型可以多元，結果不必等價。

而這也把我們帶到一個更難的問題：既然模型本來就不是世界，我們憑什麼說某個模型「比較好」？

When two maps both work, how do you choose?

兩張地圖都能用的時候，怎麼選

Admitting multiple models creates a practical nuisance: the same phenomenon really can have two or more models that work.

A city can have a transit map, a topographic map, a population map, and a price map. A body can be described anatomically, molecularly, through systems physiology, psychologically, and through social relations. A company can be seen as a balance sheet, a process network, a power structure, a talent market, or a cultural community.

Different models do not imply that one of them must be false. So how do we stop "it depends" from becoming an evasion?

A few things can be compared. Whether they answer the same question. Whether their predictions hold up on new data. Whether the explanation supports intervention. How many assumptions each one uses. Whether its failures are easy to see. How much it costs to use. Whether the cost of its errors is bearable.

Those criteria do not add themselves up into a single score. High-risk engineering weights reliability more heavily; exploratory research may care more about explanatory power and generating new hypotheses. A universal leaderboard does not exist. What needs to exist is a reason you can check: why this map.

承認多模型之後會出現一個實務上的麻煩：同一個現象真的可能有兩套甚至更多模型都能工作。

城市可以有捷運圖、地形圖、人口圖和房價圖。人體可以用解剖、分子、系統生理、心理和社會關係來描述。公司可以被看成資產負債表、流程網路、權力結構、人才市場或文化共同體。

模型不同，不代表其中一張一定是假的。那我們怎麼避免「看情況」變成一句逃避？

至少可以比幾件事：它回答的問題是否相同；在新資料上的預測是否穩定；解釋能不能支持干預；它用了多少假設；失效容不容易被看見；使用成本多高；錯誤代價能不能承受。

這些判準沒辦法自動加總成一個總分。高風險工程會給可靠性更高的權重，探索性研究可能更重視解釋力和新假設的產出。宇宙通用的排行榜並不存在。需要存在的是一個可以被檢查的理由：為什麼選這張地圖。

Multiple models need governance, not a collection

多模型需要治理，不只是收藏

Organisations often say they value multiple perspectives, and what actually happens is that each department files a report and the same single indicator decides at the end.

Having several maps on the table is not the point. The point is knowing which map holds decision rights on which question, and what happens when models conflict.

When the safety model and the revenue model disagree, do certain risks carry a veto? When a short-horizon forecasting model and a long-horizon mechanism model disagree, which one runs live operations and which one sets strategy? When an expert's judgement on a case conflicts with a statistical model, under what conditions is a manual override allowed?

Once models genuinely enter decisions, these stop being philosophical decoration and become governance.

Maturity in a multiple-model world is not measured by whether everybody has their own opinion. It is measured by whether we know where different views each have standing, and where they have to check each other.

組織常說自己重視多元觀點，實際運作卻是每個部門各交一份報告，最後仍然由同一個指標決定。

多模型的重點在於知道哪張地圖在哪個問題上有決策權，以及模型互相衝突時怎麼處理。桌上同時擺五張地圖不算。

安全模型和營收模型衝突時，是否有某些風險具有否決權？短期預測模型和長期機制模型衝突時，哪一個負責即時操作、哪一個負責策略？專家的個案判斷和統計模型衝突時，允許人工覆寫的條件是什麼？

一旦模型真正進入決策，這些都不是哲學裝飾，而是治理問題。

一個多模型世界的成熟度，不看「每個人是否都有自己的看法」。它看的是我們知不知道：不同看法在哪裡各自有資格，在哪裡必須互相制衡。

An incident where "only the interface changed"

一次「只有介面變了」的事故

The story below is several cases I have seen combined into one, with details altered. The shape of it is common.

A logistics company had a warehouse system that had been running for seven years. Floor staff scanned barcodes, confirmed locations, and the system decided the next task. For a picker, the screen had three main buttons: accept, complete, exception. The interface was minimal and a new hire was productive in half a day.

That autumn a release simplified the exception path by one more step. Previously, pressing exception meant choosing a reason: out of stock, wrong location, damaged barcode, equipment fault. The new version kept a single button and let rules classify the type afterwards. The reasoning was solid. One fewer interaction shortens handling time and removes the chance of picking the wrong reason.

At first the numbers really did improve. Average task time fell about nine per cent and operator errors fell as well.

Three weeks later something odd showed up: the stock ledger for a few zones would not reconcile. The system showed no mass failures, and the exception rate was in fact lower than before. The operations team spent a fortnight on it, revised the rules twice, and the ledger still would not balance.

The cause, when they found it, was neither the pickers nor the algorithm. Those irritating exception categories had been doing a second job all along: they were the channel through which the floor sent context back into the system. Somebody would choose "wrong location" and write in the note field that the labels on this row looked reprinted. Somebody would choose "damaged barcode" three days running, and purchasing would learn that a supplier's label stock had a problem. After the interface was simplified, that information did not disappear. It lost its entrance. The automatic rules could only guess within the existing categories, so a new kind of location-labelling problem got absorbed into whichever old category sat closest. Each individual absorption looked reasonable, and the accumulation left the maintenance team unable to see a new pattern growing.

The lesson worth keeping is not "do not simplify." The old interface had real problems, and human classification makes mistakes too. It sits in another sentence: a field, a button, a category is frequently serving several purposes at once. What you think you deleted was friction, and you may have deleted a sensor along with it.

Good abstractions therefore need to know their own second function. The surface function is making the normal path faster. The hidden function may be letting exceptions become visible, letting floor knowledge travel upward, letting somebody in the future trace things back. Optimise only the first and the system usually does not break immediately. It gradually loses its senses.

This is why I came to care about the return ticket. Encapsulation can spare people from understanding everything underneath, and it should keep one path open, so that an exception can pierce the encapsulation and be described again. Otherwise a successful interface slowly turns itself into a black box, and a black box is at its most dangerous the first time it meets a world it has not seen.

下面這個故事是我把幾個看過的案子併在一起寫的，細節做過改動，情節本身很常見。

某家物流公司有一套跑了七年的倉儲系統。現場人員每天掃條碼、確認貨位，系統自動決定下一個任務。對揀貨員來說，畫面上只有三個主要按鈕：接受、完成、異常。介面極簡，新人半天就能上線。

那年秋天改版，產品團隊把「異常」又簡化了一步。過去按下異常之後，人員還要選一個原因：缺貨、位置錯誤、條碼受損、設備故障。新版只留一個按鈕，之後由系統用規則自動判斷類型。理由很充分：少一步操作可以縮短處理時間，也避免人員選錯。

一開始數字真的變漂亮。平均任務時間下降百分之九，操作錯誤也下降。

三週後出現一個奇怪的現象：某幾個貨區的庫存帳一直對不起來。系統看不出大量故障，異常率甚至比改版前更低。維運團隊查了兩個禮拜，換過兩版規則，帳還是對不上。

最後找出來的原因，不在揀貨員身上，也不在演算法本身。那批「麻煩的異常分類」其實一直在做第二件事：它們是現場把脈絡送回系統的通道。有人選了「位置錯誤」但在備註裡寫「這一排的標籤好像重印過」；有人連續三天選「條碼受損」，於是採購知道某家供應商的標籤紙有問題。介面被簡化之後，這些資訊並沒有消失，它只是失去了入口。自動規則只能在既有的類別裡推測，遇到新型態的貨位標示問題時，就把它吸收進最接近的舊類別。每一次都看起來合理，累積起來卻讓維護團隊看不見一個正在長大的新模式。

這個故事最值得記住的地方並不是「不要簡化」。舊介面確實有問題，人的分類也會出錯。教訓在另一句話：一個欄位、一個按鈕、一個分類，往往同時服務好幾個目的。你以為自己刪掉的是摩擦，實際上可能連感測器一起刪掉了。

好的抽象因此需要知道自己的第二功能。表面功能是讓正常流程變快，隱藏功能可能是讓例外被看見、讓現場知識往上傳、讓未來的人能回溯。當我們只最佳化第一個功能，系統通常不會立刻壞掉，它會慢慢失去感覺。

這也是我後來很在意「回程票」的原因。封裝可以讓日常工作不必理解全部底層，至少要留一條路，讓例外能穿透封裝重新被描述。否則一個成功的介面會慢慢把自己變成黑箱，而黑箱最危險的時刻，通常正是它第一次遇到沒看過的世界。

Part Two

The Lifespan of a Model

A model succeeding does not mean it succeeds on every question, and every successful simplification may be filing away context that will be needed later. Part Two starts with abstraction debt: how a model can become so useful that we lose the ability to look underneath it. Then it takes on the difference between useful and true, the domain of validity, and how counterexamples ought to enter a process of revision.

第二部

模型的壽命

一套模型能成功，不代表它在所有問題上都能成功；而每一次成功的簡化，都可能把未來需要的脈絡先收進抽屜。第二部從「抽象債」開始：模型如何因為太好用而讓我們失去往下看的能力；接著處理有用與為真的差別、有效域，以及反例應該怎麼進入更新機制。

4 — Abstraction Debt

第四章　抽象債

We like a tool precisely because it spares us from knowing much. The bill usually does not arrive that day.

我們喜歡一個工具，往往正因為它讓我們不必知道太多。而帳單通常不會在那一天寄來。

On the evening of 31 May 2009, Air France flight 447 left Rio de Janeiro for Paris with two hundred and twenty-eight people on board.

Around two in the morning the aircraft was at thirty-five thousand feet over the Atlantic, crossing a band of thunderstorms near the equator. The captain was resting in the back; two co-pilots were in the cockpit. At that point ice crystals at altitude blocked the pitot tubes and the aircraft lost any trustworthy airspeed reading.

The autopilot disconnected as designed and handed the aircraft back to human hands. The flight control system dropped out of its normal mode at the same time, which is to say the layer that ordinarily prevents a stall stopped functioning.

What happened over the next three and a half minutes was later reconstructed second by second by the French investigators. The co-pilot flying pulled back on the stick. The aircraft climbed, then stalled. The stall warning sounded and the aircraft descended at more than ten thousand feet a minute with the nose held up. By the time the captain reached the cockpit it was very hard to read from the instruments what state the aircraft was in. It struck the ocean at fourteen minutes past two.

The final report, published in July 2012, does not push the blame onto any single link. It names several things at once: the crew had little training in manual handling at altitude; the stall warning stops at very low airspeeds because the instruments are no longer valid in that range; the alerting design made the situation hard to read; and something more fundamental — the automation on this type works extremely well almost all of the time, so "the autopilot has just handed the aircraft back to you" is a situation a pilot may meet once or twice in a career.

What keeps me up about this is not that automation is unreliable. The automation on that aircraft was highly reliable. It is that moment of handing back: the system returned control at the instant context mattered most, and the context it had been holding on our behalf for years did not come back with it.

Press a button and the background is removed from a photo. Call a function and thousands of lines underneath start working. A dashboard turns green and a manager knows things are normal. These things count as civilisation because they carry complexity for us. If sending a message required first understanding radio, silicon, operating systems, and encoding, modern life would not turn over.

So the question was never whether abstraction is good. Without abstraction nobody gets through a single day. The danger sits elsewhere: an abstraction that succeeds for a long time makes us gradually forget what it hid, and when those hidden differences start deciding outcomes again, we discover we lack more than the answer. We lack the entrance back into the problem.

I want to call this state abstraction debt.

二〇〇九年五月三十一日晚上，法國航空四四七號班機從里約熱內盧起飛，飛往巴黎。機上兩百二十八人。

凌晨兩點左右，飛機在大西洋上空三萬五千呎，穿過赤道附近的一片雷雨區。機長正在後方休息，駕駛艙裡是兩位副駕駛。這時機外的空速管被高空冰晶堵住，飛機失去了可信的空速讀數。

自動駕駛依照設計斷開，把飛機交回人手上。飛行控制系統同時退出正常模式，也就是說，平常會替飛行員擋住失速的那層保護，不再作用。

接下來三分半鐘裡發生的事，後來被法國調查局逐秒重建。負責操作的副駕駛把操縱桿往後拉，飛機爬升，然後失速。失速警報響起，飛機以每分鐘超過一萬呎的速度往下掉，機頭卻一直保持上仰。機長回到駕駛艙時，已經很難從儀表上看出這架飛機到底處在什麼狀態。飛機在兩點十四分撞上海面。

二〇一二年七月的最終報告不把責任推給任何單一環節。它同時指出好幾件事：組員對高空手動操作缺乏訓練，失速警報在極低空速時會停止（因為儀器在那個範圍內不再有效），警示設計讓人難以判斷，以及一個更根本的問題——這型飛機的自動化在絕大多數時候都運作得非常好，以至於「自動駕駛把飛機交還給你」這種情況，飛行員一輩子可能只遇到一兩次。

這件事真正讓我睡不著的地方，不是自動化不可靠。這型飛機的自動化非常可靠。讓我不安的是那個交還的瞬間：系統在最需要脈絡的一刻把控制權交回來，而它替我們保管了那麼多年的脈絡，並沒有跟著一起交回來。

一個按鈕按下去，照片就被去背；一個函式呼叫，數千行底層程式開始工作；儀表板亮起綠燈，管理者就知道目前正常。這些東西之所以算文明，正因為它們替我們承擔了複雜度。如果每次傳訊息都要先理解無線電、晶片、作業系統和編碼，現代生活根本轉不起來。

所以問題從來不是「抽象好不好」。沒有抽象，人連一天都活不完。危險的是另一件事：一套抽象如果長期成功，我們會逐漸忘記它藏了什麼；等到那些被藏起來的差異重新決定結果，我們才發現自己不只缺答案，甚至缺少重新理解問題的入口。

我想把這種狀態叫做「抽象債」。

A debt that was not incurred out of laziness

一筆不是因為偷懶才欠下的債

"Technical debt" has a clear origin. In 1992, at a conference on object-oriented programming, the programmer Ward Cunningham submitted a short experience report about a portfolio management system he had built. He used borrowing to describe a phenomenon: to hit the delivery speed in front of you, adopt a design that is not ideal but works, and pay a little interest on every future change; keep not repaying and the interest eventually consumes your development speed. His emphasis was on remembering to repay, rather than on not borrowing.

Abstraction debt resembles it without being the same thing.

In some software and machine learning engineering discussions, "abstraction debt" already refers to badly designed abstraction layers, rigid abstraction boundaries, or tools that invent their own unfamiliar concepts and thereby raise the cost of using and evolving them. The term has no single cross-field definition at present. I am borrowing it here for a broader problem about knowledge: to make something operable we file part of the context into an abstraction layer; when the environment changes, the filed material starts deciding outcomes again, and we have lost the ability to retrieve it.

What is owed here is not knowledge of the substrate. Nobody needs to know every substrate. You can write good code without understanding compilers, use a phone without understanding electromagnetism, deploy a model without understanding every parameter. The debt sits somewhere else: you do not know what you do not know, and the system kept no path for you to follow downward when you need to.

「技術債」這個說法有明確的出處。一九九二年，程式設計師沃德・康寧漢在一場物件導向程式設計的年會上提交了一份很短的經驗報告，講他做的一套投資組合管理系統。他用借貸來描述一種現象：為了趕上眼前的交付速度，先採用一個不理想但能工作的設計，未來每次修改都要多付一點利息；如果一直不還，最後利息會吃掉整個開發速度。他強調的重點是「要記得還」，而不是「不要借」。

抽象債和它相似，卻不完全一樣。

在一些軟體與機器學習工程的討論裡，「abstraction debt」已經被用來指抽象層設計不當、抽象邊界僵化，或者工具自己造了一套陌生概念而增加使用與演化成本。這個詞目前並沒有一個跨領域、完全統一的定義。我在這本書裡借用它，指向一個更廣的認知問題：為了讓某件事變得可以操作，我們把一部分上下文收進抽象層；當環境改變，那些被收起來的東西重新決定結果，我們卻失去了取回它們的能力。

這裡欠下的並不是「底層知識」。沒有人需要知道所有底層。你可以不懂編譯器也寫得出好程式，不懂電磁學也照樣用手機，不懂每一個參數也部署得了模型。債務發生在另一個地方：你不知道自己不知道什麼，而且系統也沒有留下一條讓你在必要時往下追的路。

The debt grows fastest when things run smoothly

順的時候，債長得最快

An interface that fails every day does not earn much trust. The awkward case is the one that has not failed for three years. After three years the interface stops being experienced as an interface at all and starts feeling like the world.

This is the same thing as the warehouse system in the last chapter. When the exception path was compressed into one button, the team gained speed and lost the channel that carried context back from the floor. The numbers improving for a few weeks did not mean complexity had decreased. It meant complexity had been moved somewhere that did not charge yet. When a new kind of problem appeared, the bill came back.

Abstraction debt therefore has a counter-intuitive property: it tends to accumulate while the system is running at its best. Success lowers the motivation to look downward, and it leads organisations to delete, one step at a time, the redundant knowledge, the exception fields, the human judgement, and the context records that look unnecessary. Each deletion is reasonable in the moment. The risk only becomes visible when some future exception that does not yet have a name shows up.

如果一個介面每天都出錯，人反而不會太相信它。麻煩的是它連續三年都沒出錯。三年之後，介面不再被感覺成「一種介面」，它變得像世界本身。

這和上一章那套倉儲系統是同一件事。當「異常」被簡化成一個按鈕，團隊得到的是速度，失去的是現場脈絡回傳的通道。前幾週數字變好，並不代表複雜度真的減少，只代表複雜度被搬到一個暫時不必付錢的地方。等新型態的問題出現，帳單才寄回來。

抽象債因此有一個反直覺的特徵：它常常在系統運作最順的時候累積。成功會降低人往下看的動機，也會讓組織一步一步刪掉那些「看起來沒必要」的備援知識、例外欄位、人工判斷和脈絡紀錄。每一次刪除當下都很合理，風險要等到未來某個還沒有名字的例外出現才會被看見。

McNamara's data room

麥納馬拉的資料室

In January 1961, Kennedy appointed a man who had been president of Ford Motor for a few weeks as Secretary of Defense. During the war Robert McNamara had worked in statistical control, analysing the efficiency of bomber missions for the American air forces; afterwards he joined Ford and used the same methods to pull a company close to losing control back onto its rails. What he brought into the Pentagon was a full apparatus of managing by numbers, along with a group of young analysts who became known as the Whiz Kids.

In many places this worked. The defence budget acquired, for the first time, a basis on which the services could be compared, and procurement decisions started to carry cost-benefit analysis. Then came Vietnam.

The popular version of the story says the American military looked only at body count and therefore lost. That version is too tidy. The statistics collected at the time were staggering in volume: enemy losses, weapons captured, road trafficability, proportion of territory controlled. In 1967 a hamlet evaluation system was introduced that scored more than ten thousand hamlets in South Vietnam every month on security, political, and economic conditions, generating data by the million. The historian Gregory Daddis has argued that part of the problem came from having too many indicators — so many that nobody could judge which one actually meant anything.

That correction makes the example more important, not less. Real abstraction debt does not need a stupid indicator to happen. You can have a hundred dashboards, a thousand fields, and clean trend lines, and still measure the wrong thing with great precision. Once political legitimacy, popular support, local networks, and the other side's capacity to mobilise get pushed to the margins of the reporting, a decision system can grow further from the war it wants to understand while its data grows more complete.

In 1995 McNamara published a memoir and acknowledged that many of the reports used to measure progress had been misleading. What is worth keeping here is not "data management lost the war," which is both too simple and unfair. It is a more general regularity: once a representational system becomes the main interface for allocating resources and tracking accountability, people start reshaping the world into a form that interface can read.

This is also the bridge between abstraction debt and Chapter 10. An abstraction starts out describing. Connect it to power and it starts producing the thing it only meant to measure.

一九六一年一月，甘迺迪讓一位剛當上福特汽車總裁沒幾個星期的人接任國防部長。羅伯・麥納馬拉在二戰期間做的是統計管制，替美軍分析轟炸機任務的效率；戰後他進福特，用同一套方法把一家瀕臨失控的公司整理回軌道。他帶進五角大廈的，是一整套用數字管理的信念，還有一群後來被稱為「神童」的年輕分析師。

這套做法在很多地方奏效。國防預算第一次有了跨軍種可比較的基礎，採購決策開始有成本效益分析。然後越戰來了。

流行版本的故事說，美軍只看「擊殺數」這一個指標，所以輸了。這個版本太乾淨。當時軍方蒐集的統計多到嚇人：敵軍損失、武器繳獲量、道路通行狀況、控制區域比例；一九六七年還導入了一套「村落評估系統」，每個月替南越上萬個村落打分，評估安全、政治與經濟狀況，資料量以百萬筆計。歷史學者格雷戈里・戴迪斯甚至提醒，問題有一部分來自「指標太多」，多到沒有人能判斷哪一個真正說明了什麼。

這個修正反而讓例子變得更重要。因為真正的抽象債不需要一個愚蠢的指標才會發生。你可以有一百張儀表板、一千個欄位、漂亮的趨勢圖，仍然把錯的東西量得非常精確。當政治合法性、民眾支持、地方網絡、對方的動員能力這些難以量化的因素被排到報表邊緣，決策系統就可能在資料越來越完整的同時，離它想理解的那場戰爭越來越遠。

一九九五年，麥納馬拉出版回憶錄，承認當時許多用來衡量進展的報告具有誤導性。這裡值得記住的並不是「數據管理害了越戰」——那句話太簡單，也不公平。值得記住的是一條更普遍的規律：一旦某個表示系統成為資源分配與責任追蹤的主要接口，人就會開始把世界調整成那個接口看得懂的形狀。

這也是抽象債和後面第十章之間的橋。抽象一開始只是描述；當它接上權力，就會開始生產它原本只想量測的東西。

Users are not that easily fooled

使用者並沒有那麼笨

People are not merely deceived by abstraction layers. Much of the time we are rather good at pushing a tool further than its designer imagined, without knowing the principles underneath.

You have certainly met this kind of expert. A designer who does not know how the imaging algorithm works, and knows that for a certain sort of photograph you raise the contrast before making the selection and the edges come out much cleaner. An administrator who has never heard of database normalisation, and who kept a workflow that broke slightly every day running for six years with a long chain of formulas, a few scratch columns, and paste-as-values. An engineer twenty years on a production line who cannot explain a machine's full theory, and who knows that when a particular sound appears you should stop trusting the gauges.

From the standpoint of pure architectural taste, some of these are ugly. From a cognitive standpoint they reveal something important about people: between the abstraction layer and the substrate we can grow a second-hand, experiential operating model. It is not source code and not a final theory, and it can raise control precision exactly where the model starts failing at its edges.

I call this capability edge lubrication.

Lubrication does not repair the substrate. It knows that turning this dial a little further, slowing that step down, handing a certain exception to a human, will get the system across a place where it does not run smoothly. A great deal of professional intuition, craft skill, and organisational tacit agreement has this ingredient in it.

不過人並不是只會被抽象層騙。很多時候，我們相當擅長在不知道底層原理的情況下，把工具用到比設計者想像得更遠。

你一定見過這種高手。有位設計師不知道影像演算法怎麼運作，卻知道某一類照片先把對比拉高再做選取，邊緣會乾淨很多。有位行政同事完全沒聽過資料庫正規化，卻用一長串公式、幾個暫存欄和「貼上為值」，把一套每天都會壞一點的流程維持了六年。有位在產線待了二十年的工程師講不清某台設備的完整原理，可他知道：「這個聲音一出現，先不要相信儀表板。」

從純粹的架構美學來看，這些做法有時很難看。從認知的角度看，它們揭露了人類一種很重要的能力：我們可以在抽象層和底層之間，長出一套第二手的、經驗性的操作模型。它不是原始碼，也不是終極理論，卻能在模型邊緣失效的時候提高控制精度。

我把這種能力叫做「邊緣潤滑」。

潤滑不修底層。它只是知道這個旋鈕多轉一點、那個步驟慢一點、某種例外要人工接手，就能讓系統跨過原本不順的地方。很多專業直覺、工藝技巧和組織默契，本質上都有這個成分。

Lubrication promotes itself quietly

潤滑會悄悄升格

We are inclined to revere real understanding of the substrate and to look down on workarounds. From the standpoint of bounded rationality that hierarchy is suspect. The world is too large for anybody to have time to build a complete causal model of every tool. A nurse who knows from years of experience that certain monitor readings look normal while the patient is not right, an operations engineer who knows that a particular combination of log lines means a failure is coming — those judgements can be extremely valuable even before anybody has theorised them.

What makes edge lubrication dangerous is not its impurity. It is that it promotes itself quietly. A technique that worked on one machine, one batch of data, one team succeeds so many times that people remember it as how things are. Once a local compensating model forgets its own provenance, it stops being a technique and becomes doctrine.

我們容易崇拜「真的懂底層」而看不起繞路。從有限理性的角度看，這種階級感很可疑。世界太大，沒有人有足夠時間替每一個工具建立完整的因果模型。一位護理師靠多年經驗知道某些監測數字「看起來正常但病人不對勁」，一位維運工程師知道某種日誌組合代表故障即將發生，這些判斷即使還沒有被完整理論化，仍然可能極有價值。

邊緣潤滑危險的地方在於它會悄悄升格。原本只在某一台機器、某一批資料、某一個團隊有效的技巧，因為成功太多次，被人記成「事情就是這樣」。局部補償模型一旦忘記自己的形成史，就從技巧變成教條。

Russell's chicken

羅素的雞

Push this one layer further and you arrive at the problem of induction.

In 1912 Bertrand Russell wrote a short passage in The Problems of Philosophy. A chicken is fed by a man every day, and all the evidence it gathers in its life points the same way: this man arriving means food. The regularity strengthens daily. Then one day the same man walks over and wrings its neck. Russell's point was that more refined views about the uniformity of nature would have served the chicken better.

Later textbooks in the philosophy of science rewrote it as a more dramatic turkey: fed at nine every morning, the observations accumulating, confidence in "nine o'clock means food" rising steadily, and then the regularity stops the day before Thanksgiving.

What is cruel in this story is not that induction can be wrong. Any usable knowledge can be wrong. The cruelty is that for that bird, "the man is raising me in order to kill me at the end" is not in the space of variables it can observe. It can gather weather, time, footsteps, and feed type more precisely than ever, and no field it has points at the upper-level purpose that actually determines the outcome.

I call this state structural blindness. It is a different thing from being temporarily short of a data point: we may not even have the ability to represent, in advance, which kind of data would overturn the whole model.

David Hume's version, from 1748, is stricter. His question was not whether the future will differ from the past. It was on what basis we move from "it has always been so" to "it will go on being so." If the answer is that reasoning this way has worked in the past, we are still using induction to defend induction. People do not stop predicting because of this; we still have to live, design, treat patients, do science. What Hume removed is one kind of over-confidence: past success cannot supply a logical guarantee.

把這件事再往下推一層，就會碰到歸納問題。

一九一二年，伯特蘭・羅素在《哲學問題》裡寫了一段很短的話。他說，一隻雞每天被人餵食，牠一生累積的證據都指向同一個結論：這個人來了就有東西吃。這個規律一天比一天穩固。然後有一天，同一個人走過來，扭斷了牠的脖子。羅素用這個例子指出：「關於自然一致性的比較細緻的看法，對這隻雞來說會比較有用。」

後來的科學哲學教材把牠改寫成一隻更戲劇化的火雞：每天早上九點被餵食，觀測資料越來越多，對「九點會被餵」的信心越來越高；偏偏在感恩節前一天，規律停止了。

這個故事殘酷的地方，並不在「歸納會犯錯」。所有可用的知識都可能犯錯。殘酷的是：對那隻雞來說，「主人養牠是為了最後宰掉牠」根本不在牠可以觀察的變數空間裡。牠可以把天氣、時間、腳步聲、飼料種類都收集得更精確，仍然沒有任何一個欄位指向真正決定結果的那個上層目的。

我把這個狀態叫做「結構性盲目」。它跟「暫時少收集一筆資料」是兩件不同的事：我們連「哪一種資料會推翻整個模型」都未必有能力事先表示出來。

大衛・休謨在一七四八年提出的版本更嚴格。他問的是另一句話：我們憑什麼從「過去一直如此」推出「未來仍會如此」？如果答案是「因為過去這樣推都很成功」，那還是在用歸納替歸納辯護。人當然不會因此停止預測，我們還是要生活、要設計、要治療、要做科學。休謨拆掉的只是一種過度自信：過去的成功本身，沒辦法在邏輯上提供絕對保證。

Unknowns with no box to put them in

沒有格子的未知

We usually picture the unknown as a question mark: the answer has not been filled in, and at least the box has been drawn. Structural blindness is more awkward. It says some unknowns have no box.
